intro: The ship was crushed by pack ice in the first winter, and the sea has kept its silence ever since. What survives of the expedition is a biscuit tin full of messages, each written in a different hand, and each deliberately obscure. We huddle in the canvas of base camp, the wind rattling the walls, while the tin sits on the low wooden table like a reluctant oracle. The old charts are tacked to the wall, their margins stained with tea, and a brass thimble rests beside them, its tiny opening aimed at the edge of the map as though it knew which word of each message should be drawn. When the fire finally yields a spark, we read the notes aloud, hoping the answer lies not in what is said but in the quiet habit of the camp that has kept them together.
echo: The river behind the tents moves a foot a day, and it is made of ice.

puzzles.title: Sastrugi
puzzles.flavor: Some squares have been given to you for free.
puzzles.hint: A nonogram (paint-by-numbers). The filled picture is the answer written in 5×5 block letters.

puzzles.title: Whiteout
puzzles.flavor: Heard over the radio from the other side of the glass.
puzzles.hint: NATO phonetic alphabet, then Atbash (A↔Z, B↔Y, ...).

puzzles.title: Polar Plateau
puzzles.flavor: A paint chart for a room nobody will ever decorate. Alpha and Omega traded places before this was written down.

partials.c2b0b080adf2e9675388ec85ae67ec047d9f2238: You've decoded it, but it's not finished. One more layer.

puzzles.hint: Each hex colour code is three ASCII bytes. Then undo: Atbash (A↔Z mirror).

puzzles.title: Katabatic
puzzles.hint: The sentence was cut into three-letter fragments (spaces removed) and alphabetised. Reassemble it using the word lengths; it tells you the answer.

puzzles.title: Nunatak
puzzles.flavor: A negative, hung upside down, of something that only reads in threes.
puzzles.hint: This is the template (antisense) strand written 5′→3′. Reverse-complement it to get the coding strand, then translate codons to amino-acid one-letter codes.
